about: Programming for Engineers (ELEC40004) is the 10-ECTS Year 1 programming module shared by Imperial's EEE and EIE degrees, compulsory and running across the Autumn and Spring terms (2026-27 module catalogue). It teaches C++ from scratch, assuming no previous programming. The department's intranet course page (undated, so it may describe an earlier year) says Term 1 covers core imperative programming (control flow and data structures) and Term 2 covers encapsulation, object-oriented programming and the design of larger software; the topics here follow its syllabus list, with variables, control flow and functions drawn out as a topic from its aims and learning outcomes. That page lists assessment as 100% coursework with no end-of-year exam: programming assignments (80%) and a team project (20%); check your current module handbook, as this may have changed.

Implementing data structures: vectors, lists and trees

cards.b: It is a preprocessor directive that inserts the declarations of the standard I/O library (std::cin, std::cout, std::endl) into the file before compilation.
The compiler turns each source file into object code after checking syntax and types; the linker combines object files and libraries into one executable and reports undefined references.
The return value of main is passed to the operating system; 0 conventionally means the program finished successfully, non-zero signals an error.
Extraction stops at whitespace, so word becomes "Ada"; "Lovelace" stays in the input buffer for the next read. Use std::getline to read the whole line.
An error where the program compiles and runs but produces the wrong result. Neither the compiler nor the runtime detects it; only testing against known answers does.
Turns on a broad set of compiler warnings (for example unused variables or comparisons between signed and unsigned), helping you find likely bugs before running the code.
If extraction fails (e.g. letters read into an int), the stream's fail flag is set and later reads do nothing until std::cin.clear() is called and the bad input is discarded.
7 / 2 is 3 (integer division truncates) and 7 % 2 is 1 (remainder). 7 / 2.0 is 3.5 because one operand is a double.
The function receives a copy of the argument; changes inside the function do not affect the caller's variable.
The parameter is an alias for the caller's variable, so the function can modify it and no copy is made.

cards.f: Why pass large objects by const reference?
cards.b: It avoids copying (faster, less memory) while the const guarantees the function cannot modify the caller's object.
while tests the condition first and may run zero times; do-while runs the body once before testing, so it always executes at least once.
It assigns 5 to x and then tests the value 5, which is true, so the branch always runs. Comparison needs ==.
The region of code where a name is valid: a variable declared inside a block { } exists only from its declaration to the end of that block.

cards.f: Why compare doubles with a tolerance?
cards.b: Floating-point arithmetic is approximate (0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3), so test std::abs(a - b) < epsilon rather than a == b.
File stream classes from <fstream>: ifstream reads from a file and ofstream writes to one, using the same >> and << operators as cin and cout.
If the file is missing or the path is wrong the stream fails silently and every read fails; checking lets the program report the error and stop.

eof is set only when a read tries to go past the end of the file. With a trailing newline the last good read leaves eof false, so the loop runs once more, the read fails and the last value is processed twice. Use while (f >> x) instead.
Open with std::ofstream f("log.txt", std::ios::app); the default mode truncates the existing contents.
Reads characters up to (and discarding) the next newline into a std::string, so spaces are kept; returns the stream, which is false at end of input.
A stream built on a string (from <sstream>): lets you use >> to split one line read by getline into separate fields.
Makes the file in.txt act as std::cin and sends std::cout to out.txt, so a console program can be tested on files without code changes.
Indexing v[i] is O(1) because elements are contiguous; push_back is amortised O(1) because capacity grows geometrically when the vector is full.

cards.f: Insert at the front of a vector
cards.b: O(n): every existing element must be shifted one place to make room.
O(log n); a map keeps keys sorted and is typically implemented as a balanced binary search tree (red-black tree).
A hash-table container with average O(1) insertion and lookup; keys are not kept in any order.
An iterator one past the last element. It must not be dereferenced; it marks the end of the half-open range [begin, end).
Both return element i, but at(i) checks the index and throws std::out_of_range if invalid, while [] does no check (undefined behaviour if out of range).
A push_back that triggers reallocation moves all elements, so existing iterators, pointers and references into the vector become invalid.

cards.f: What does counts[key]++ do for a new key in std::map<string,int>?
cards.b: operator[] inserts the key with a value-initialised int (0), then ++ makes it 1. Use find or count to test membership without inserting.
A user-defined type that groups named members, possibly of different types, into one object, e.g. struct Point { double x; double y; };
obj.member accesses a member of an object; ptr->member accesses a member through a pointer and means (*ptr).member.

cards.f: Only language difference between struct and class
cards.b: Default access: struct members (and base classes) are public by default; class members are private by default.

cards.f: Why prefer a vector of structs to parallel arrays?
cards.b: Each record's fields stay together, so sorting, inserting or deleting cannot misalign them; the code is clearer and easier to pass to functions.
A function returning true if a should come before b, e.g. return a.ohms < b.ohms; It must be a strict ordering, so use < rather than <=.
Initialising a simple struct with braces in member order, e.g. Point p = {3, 4}; sets p.x = 3 and p.y = 4.
A scoped enumeration defining a type with named values, e.g. enum class Mode { Off, On }; safer than plain ints because values do not convert implicitly to int.
Bundling data with the functions that operate on it and restricting outside access (private members), so the object controls its own state and can maintain its invariants.
Exposing what an object does through a simple interface while hiding how it is implemented, so users rely on behaviour, not internal details.
A condition that must be true for every valid object between member function calls, e.g. 0 ≤ mins ≤ 59; constructors establish it and member functions preserve it.
A member function with the class's name and no return type that runs when an object is created; it initialises members and establishes the invariant.
Declared with const after the parameter list; it promises not to modify the object's data and it can be called on a const object, whereas non-const member functions cannot.
Syntax after a constructor's parameter list, e.g. : w(w), h(h), which initialises members directly before the constructor body runs.
~ClassName(), called automatically when an object is destroyed; used to release resources such as heap memory or file handles.

cards.f: Benefit of private data when changing representation
cards.b: Outside code only uses the public interface, so the internal data layout can change without any change to client code (it may need recompiling, but not rewriting).
The address-of operator: gives a pointer to x. In a declaration such as int& r = x; the & instead declares a reference.
Dereference: the object that pointer p points to. Reading or writing *p accesses that object; dereferencing nullptr is undefined behaviour.
When an array is passed to a function or assigned to a pointer it converts to a pointer to its first element, losing its size information.
delete[]. Memory from new is freed with delete; mixing the two forms is undefined behaviour.
Heap memory that is never freed because the program has lost every pointer to it; the memory stays allocated until the program ends.
A pointer that still holds the address of memory that has been freed or of a local variable that no longer exists; using it is undefined behaviour.

cards.f: Pointer arithmetic: q + 2 for int* q
cards.b: Advances by two ints (2 × sizeof(int) bytes), so if q points to arr[0], q + 2 points to arr[2] and *(q + 2) == q[2].
A smart pointer from <memory> that owns a heap object and deletes it automatically when the unique_ptr is destroyed, preventing leaks (RAII).
A struct holding a value and a pointer to the next node; the list is a head pointer, and nullptr marks the end.

cards.f: Linked list: cost of insert at head vs access k-th element
cards.b: Insert at head is O(1) (create node, point it at old head); accessing the k-th element is O(k), i.e. O(n), because you must follow k links.
For every node, all keys in its left subtree are smaller and all keys in its right subtree are larger than the node's key.
Visit left subtree, node, then right subtree; for a BST it outputs the keys in ascending order.

cards.f: Worst-case BST height and when it occurs
cards.b: n counting nodes, or n − 1 counting edges (a chain), e.g. when keys are inserted already sorted; search and insert then become O(n) instead of O(log n).

cards.f: Why post-order to delete a tree?
cards.b: Children are deleted before their parent, so the parent's child pointers are still valid when visited; deleting the parent first would lose access to the subtrees.
When full, allocate a larger array (e.g. double the capacity), copy elements across, delete[] the old array; geometric growth gives amortised O(1) push_back.
If a class needs a user-written destructor, copy constructor or copy assignment operator (usually because it owns raw resources), it almost certainly needs all three.
The case a recursive function answers directly without calling itself; it stops the recursion. Every recursive path must eventually reach it.
Each call uses a new stack frame; if recursion never reaches a base case (or goes too deep) the call stack runs out of space and the program crashes.
The data must be sorted; each comparison halves the remaining range, so it takes O(log n) comparisons.
It gives the same midpoint as (lo + hi) / 2 but cannot overflow int when lo and hi are both large.
O(n log n) in all cases: log₂ n levels of halving, with O(n) merging work per level. It needs O(n) extra memory.
Exponential (grows roughly like 1.618ⁿ) because the same subproblems are recomputed; memoisation or a loop reduces it to O(n).
Bubble sort, selection sort and insertion sort in the worst case: nested loops compare roughly n²/2 pairs.
Split a problem into smaller subproblems of the same kind, solve them recursively, and combine the results (e.g. merge sort, binary search).
class D : public B means D is a kind of B: it inherits B's members and can add new ones or override virtual functions.
A member function whose call through a base pointer or reference is resolved at run time using the object's actual type, enabling polymorphism.
A virtual function declared with = 0 that need not have a base implementation, e.g. virtual double area() const = 0; derived classes must override it to be instantiable.
A class with at least one pure virtual function. You cannot create objects of it, but you can have pointers and references to it.

cards.f: Why a virtual destructor in a base class?
cards.b: So that deleting a derived object through a base-class pointer runs the derived destructor too; without it the behaviour is undefined and resources may leak.
Copying a derived object into a base-class object by value keeps only the base part; derived data and overridden behaviour are lost.
Marks a member function as overriding a base virtual function; the compiler reports an error if no matching virtual function exists (e.g. a const or spelling mismatch).
Inheritance models "is a" (a Circle is a Shape); composition models "has a" by making one object a member of another (a Circuit has Components).

questions.q: A program compiles without errors but the linker reports "undefined reference to compute(int)". What is the most likely cause?
options: compute was declared but its definition was never compiled into the program
There is a missing semicolon in the line that calls compute
compute was called with a double instead of an int
The program forgot to return 0 from main
questions.why: Undefined references are linker errors: a declaration let the call compile, but no compiled definition exists to link against. A missing semicolon is a syntax error caught by the compiler, passing a double to an int parameter is converted implicitly and compiles, and main may omit return (it then returns 0 implicitly).

a reads 12 successfully. Reading "abc" into an int fails, which sets the fail state; since C++11 a failed numeric extraction stores 0 in b, which was already 0 here anyway. The text "abc" can never be printed from an int, and the code is valid C++ so it compiles.

questions.q: Explain the difference between compile-time, run-time and logic errors, giving a C++ example of each, and say how each is usually detected.
markScheme: Compile-time: violates language rules (e.g. missing semicolon, undeclared variable); detected by compiler messages
Run-time: builds but fails when executed (e.g. division by zero, invalid pointer dereference, out-of-range access); detected by crashes, sanitisers or a debugger
Logic: runs but gives wrong output (e.g. using < instead of <= in a loop bound); detected only by testing against expected results
Clear statement of how testing with known inputs and edge cases finds logic errors
questions.modelAnswer: A compile-time error breaks the rules of C++, so the compiler refuses to produce an executable: for example writing int x = 5 without a semicolon, or using a variable that was never declared. The compiler's message points to the line. A run-time error occurs when a program that compiled successfully does something invalid while running, such as dividing an integer by zero or dereferencing a null pointer; it usually shows up as a crash, and tools such as a debugger or address sanitiser help locate it. A logic error is the hardest: the program runs normally but the result is wrong, for instance a loop written for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) that misses the last element. Only testing with inputs whose correct outputs are known, including edge cases, reveals logic errors.

questions.why: The loop runs for i = 1, 2, 3, 4; continue skips even values, so s = 1 + 3 = 4. The total 10 would include every value 1 to 4, 6 is the sum of the even values 2 + 4, and 9 would wrongly include 5, which fails the test i < 5.

a is passed by value, so only a copy of x is incremented and x stays 1; b is a reference to y, so y becomes 2. Both changing would need both parameters to be references, neither changing would need both to be values, and x changing alone would need the opposite parameter types.

questions.q: Write a C++ function int count_digits(int n) that returns the number of decimal digits in a non-negative integer n (count_digits(0) should return 1). Then state the result of count_digits(4096) and explain how you would test the function.
markScheme: Correct signature and handling of n == 0 returning 1
Loop that divides n by 10 until it reaches 0, incrementing a counter
Returns the counter; count_digits(4096) gives 4
Test plan includes 0, single-digit, boundary values such as 9/10/99/100 and a large value

questions.q: A file contains the three lines 5, 7 and 9, each ending with a newline. Which loop sums exactly 5 + 7 + 9 = 21?
options: int x, s = 0; while (f >> x) { s += x; }
int x, s = 0; while (!f.eof()) { f >> x; s += x; }
int x, s = 0; do { f >> x; s += x; } while (f >> x);
int x, s = 0; f >> x; while (f) { s += x; }
questions.why: Testing the extraction itself stops as soon as a read fails, so each value is added once. The eof-controlled loop adds the final 9 a second time (total 30): after 9 is read the newline is still unread, so eof is false, the next read fails and leaves x at 9, the do-while version reads twice per iteration and skips every other value, and the last version never reads again inside the loop, so it never ends.

questions.q: What happens when a program runs std::ofstream out("results.txt"); and results.txt already exists?
options: The existing contents are discarded and the file starts empty
New output is added after the existing contents
The program throws an exception because the file exists
The stream opens in read-only mode
questions.why: The default mode for an output file stream truncates the file. Adding to the end requires std::ios::app, streams do not throw by default when opening, and an ofstream is for writing, not reading.

questions.q: A file sensors.txt has one record per line: a sensor name (no spaces) followed by a temperature in °C. Write a C++ fragment that reads the file, ignores malformed lines, and prints the name of the hottest sensor. Explain one design choice.
markScheme: Opens an ifstream and checks it opened successfully
Reads line by line with getline and parses with a stringstream (or uses file >> name >> temp in the loop condition)
Tracks the maximum temperature and corresponding name, initialised from the first valid record or a flag
Handles the case of no valid records
Sensible justification (e.g. getline lets bad lines be skipped without breaking the rest of the read)

questions.q: A program must store a large set of student IDs and repeatedly check whether a given ID is present; order does not matter. Which container gives the best average lookup time?
questions.why: A hash-based unordered_set has average O(1) membership tests. Searching an unsorted vector or a list is O(n), and std::set is O(log n), which is good but slower on average than hashing when ordering is not needed.

After sorting v is {1, 3, 4}; push_back adds 2 to the end giving {1, 3, 4, 2}. v[1] is 3, back() is 2 and size() is 4, printed with no separators as 324. The output 123 assumes the vector is re-sorted after the push_back, which does not happen; 3 2 4 has the right values but the code inserts no spaces; and 344 treats back() as the largest sorted element (4) rather than the newly appended 2.

questions.q: Explain how std::vector achieves amortised O(1) push_back, and why inserting at the start of a vector is O(n). Name a container you would use instead if a program constantly inserted and removed at the front.
markScheme: A vector stores elements contiguously with a capacity larger than or equal to its size
When full, it allocates a larger block (capacity grows by a constant factor), copies or moves the elements, and frees the old block
Geometric growth means total copying over n push_backs is O(n), so the average cost per push_back is O(1)
Inserting at the front shifts every existing element, which is O(n)
std::deque (or std::list) supports O(1) insertion and removal at the front
questions.modelAnswer: A vector keeps its elements in one contiguous block whose capacity can exceed the number of elements in use. push_back writes into the next free slot in O(1). When the block is full the vector allocates a new one, typically a constant factor larger (implementations commonly use 1.5 or 2), moves the elements across and frees the old block. That step costs O(n), but because capacity grows geometrically it happens rarely: over n insertions the total copying is bounded by a constant times n, so the amortised cost per push_back is O(1). Inserting at the start is different: every existing element must move up one position to make room, so each such insertion costs O(n). For frequent insertion and removal at the front I would use std::deque, which supports O(1) push_front and pop_front while still allowing indexing, or std::list if I also need to insert in the middle.

questions.q: Given struct Point { double x; double y; }; and Point* p = new Point{1, 2};, which expression reads the y member?
questions.why: p is a pointer, so the arrow operator is needed: p->y is the same as (*p).y. p.y treats the pointer as an object, *p.y is parsed as *(p.y) because . binds tighter than *, and &p->y gives the address of y, not its value.

questions.q: Which statement about C++ structs is correct?
options: A struct can have member functions and constructors, just like a class
A struct cannot be stored in a std::vector
Struct members are private by default
Assigning one struct to another copies only the first member
questions.why: In C++ a struct is a class whose members are public by default, so it can have constructors and member functions. Structs are stored in vectors all the time, private-by-default describes class, and assignment copies every member.

questions.q: Define a struct Sample holding a time in seconds and a voltage. Write a function that takes a vector of Samples and returns the time at which the largest voltage occurs, and state one reason for passing the vector by const reference.
markScheme: Correct struct with two double members and closing semicolon
Function signature taking const std::vector<Sample>& and returning double
Correct loop tracking the maximum voltage and its time (handles first element correctly)
Reason: avoids copying the whole vector while preventing modification

questions.q: Inside main, for an object c of class Counter whose member int n is declared private, which line fails to compile?
questions.why: Private members cannot be accessed from outside the class, so assigning c.n directly is a compile error. Calling the public member functions increment and value is allowed, and copying an object uses the copy constructor, which is fine.

questions.q: Why should a getter such as double get_voltage() be declared const?
options: So it can be called on const objects and the compiler checks it does not change the object
So the returned value cannot be changed by the caller
So the function runs faster because it is inlined
So the member variable becomes read-only for every other member function
questions.why: A const member function promises not to modify the object, which lets it be called through const references and has the compiler enforce the promise. It says nothing about whether the caller may change the returned copy, it does not force inlining, and other member functions can still modify the member.

questions.q: Design a class Battery for a simulation. It stores a capacity (mAh) and a current charge (mAh). The charge must always be between 0 and the capacity. Give the class declaration with a constructor, a function to draw current for a time, and a getter, and explain how your design maintains the invariant.
markScheme: Private data members for capacity and charge
Constructor validating capacity > 0 and starting charge clamped/validated to [0, capacity]
Member function draw(current_mA, hours) reducing charge by current × time and clamping at 0 (or refusing)
const getter(s) for charge or percentage
Explanation: data is private so the only way to change it is through functions that enforce 0 ≤ charge ≤ capacity
Sensible handling of invalid inputs (negative current/time)

questions.why: p starts at arr[0]; p++ moves it to arr[1]; *p += 5 changes arr[1] from 20 to 25, so the output is 10 25. 15 20 would need the update to happen before p++ moved the pointer, 16 20 comes from treating p++ as incrementing the value arr[0] (as (*p)++ would) before adding 5 to it, and 10 20 (array unchanged) ignores that *p modifies the element it points to.

questions.q: Which function returns a dangling pointer?
options: int* f() { static int x = 5; return &x; }
questions.why: x is a local variable destroyed when f returns, so its address is no longer valid. new int(5) creates a heap object that outlives the call (the caller must delete it), a static local lives for the whole program, and nullptr is a valid null value, not a dangling address.

markScheme: The array allocated with new[] is never freed, and the only pointer to it (v) is lost when the function returns
Fix 1: store result, call delete[] v before returning (delete[] not delete)
Fix 2: use std::vector<double> v(n), which frees its memory automatically
Mentions RAII or automatic destruction at end of scope as the reason the vector version cannot leak
Notes n should be positive to avoid dividing by zero

questions.q: The keys 50, 30, 70, 20, 40 are inserted in that order into an empty binary search tree. What does a pre-order traversal print?
questions.why: 50 is the root with 30 on the left (children 20 and 40) and 70 on the right. Pre-order visits node, then left subtree, then right subtree: 50 30 20 40 70. The sorted list is the in-order traversal, 20 40 30 70 50 is post-order, and 50 30 70 20 40 is the level-order (breadth-first) sequence.

questions.q:
What is wrong with this loop for freeing a linked list?
while (head != nullptr) { delete head; head = head->next; }
options: It reads head->next after head has been deleted
It frees only the first node
It should use delete[] instead of delete
questions.why: After delete head, the node's memory is no longer valid, so head->next is a use of a dangling pointer (undefined behaviour). The fix is to save next before deleting. The loop is intended to visit every node, and each node came from a single new, so delete (not delete[]) is the right form.

questions.q: Write a recursive function int count_nodes(const TreeNode* t) for a binary tree, and a function that returns the height (number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path, 0 for an empty tree). For the tree built by inserting 8, 3, 10, 1, 6, 14 into a BST, give both results.
markScheme: count_nodes: base case nullptr returns 0; otherwise 1 + count of left + count of right
height: base case nullptr returns 0; otherwise 1 + max of left and right heights
Recognises the tree shape: root 8; 3 with children 1 and 6; 10 with right child 14
count_nodes gives 6
height gives 3

questions.why: f(4) = 4 + f(3) = 4 + 3 + f(2) = 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 + f(0) = 10. Multiplying would give 24 (that would be factorial), returning just 4 ignores the recursive calls, and the base case n == 0 is reached because n decreases by one each call.

questions.q: A sorted vector has 1,000,000 elements. Roughly how many comparisons does binary search need in the worst case?
questions.why: Each comparison halves the range and 2²⁰ is about 1.05 million, so about 20 comparisons suffice. 1,000 is the square root of n, not log₂ n; 500,000 is the average for a linear search; and 1,000,000 is the worst case for a linear search.

questions.q: Write a recursive C++ function int power(int b, int e) that computes bᵉ for e ≥ 0 using the facts b⁰ = 1, bᵉ = (b^(e/2))² for even e and bᵉ = b × bᵉ⁻¹ for odd e. Trace power(2, 10) and state the number of recursive calls in big-O terms.
markScheme: Base case e == 0 returns 1
Even case computes half = power(b, e / 2) once and returns half * half
Odd case returns b * power(b, e - 1)
Correct trace giving 1024
Complexity O(log e), explained by halving at least every two calls
Notes the need to compute half once (calling power twice would lose the speed-up)

questions.why: f is not virtual, so p->f() is bound at compile time to A::f because p has type A*, printing A. g is virtual, so p->g() uses the object's real type B, printing B. BB would need f to be virtual, AA would need g to be non-virtual, and BA reverses which function is virtual.

questions.q: Shape declares virtual double area() const = 0;. Which statement is true?
options: Shape s; does not compile, but Shape* p = new Circle(1); does (if Circle overrides area)
Shape s; compiles and s.area() returns 0
Every class derived from Shape must be abstract
Pointers of type Shape* are not allowed
questions.why: A pure virtual function makes Shape abstract, so objects of Shape cannot be created, but pointers and references to it are allowed and can point at concrete derived objects. The = 0 does not mean the function returns 0, derived classes become concrete once they override every pure virtual function, and base-class pointers are exactly how polymorphism is used.

questions.q: A circuit simulator stores components in std::vector<Component*>. Component has a virtual function double impedance_mag(double f) const. Explain how virtual functions let the simulator compute every component's impedance without knowing each component's type, and give two errors a programmer could make with this design.
markScheme: Each derived class (Resistor, Capacitor, Inductor) overrides impedance_mag
Calling through Component* uses dynamic binding, so the derived version for the actual object is executed
Adding a new component type needs no change to the loop (open for extension)
Error 1: forgetting virtual in the base (static binding calls base version) or a signature mismatch without override
Error 2: no virtual destructor when deleting through Component*, or storing components by value causing slicing, or leaking raw pointers
questions.modelAnswer: Component is an abstract base class with virtual double impedance_mag(double f) const. Resistor returns R, Capacitor returns 1/(2πfC) and Inductor returns 2πfL, each overriding the base function. The simulator loops over the vector and calls c->impedance_mag(f); because the function is virtual, the call is resolved at run time from the actual object, so each component's own formula runs. The loop never names concrete types, so adding a new component class needs no change to it. Two common errors: first, leaving out virtual in the base (or slightly changing the signature in the derived class, such as forgetting const) so the base version is called; writing override makes the compiler catch the mismatch. Second, deleting the components through Component* without a virtual destructor in Component, which is undefined behaviour and can leak resources; with raw pointers someone must also remember to delete every component, which storing std::unique_ptr<Component> would handle automatically.

questions.q:
A file parts.txt lists resistors, one per line: an identifier and a value in ohms, e.g.
R2 220
R1 100
R3 470
(a) Define a suitable struct and write a function that reads the file into a std::vector, skipping non-positive values and reporting if the file cannot be opened. [6]
(b) Write functions returning the equivalent resistance if all the resistors are connected in series and if all are connected in parallel. [5]
(c) Sort the resistors by value and print the identifier of the smallest. [4]
(d) Give the program's output for the file above, and describe how you would test the program, including at least two edge cases. [5]
markScheme: (a) struct Resistor with std::string id and double ohms; read_resistors opens an ifstream, checks is_open, loops while (infile >> r.id >> r.ohms), pushes valid records
(a) Uses the extraction in the loop condition (not eof), skips ohms ≤ 0
(b) Series: sum of values
(b) Parallel: reciprocal of the sum of reciprocals (1 / Σ(1/Rᵢ)); uses floating-point division
(c) std::sort with a comparator using <, then rs.front().id (or std::min_element)
(d) Series 790 Ω, parallel ≈ 59.98 Ω, smallest R1
(d) Testing: hand-computed cases such as two equal resistors (parallel = R/2), single resistor, empty or missing file, malformed or negative lines
Code is clearly organised with const references and checks for an empty vector before dividing or calling front()

questions.q:
You are asked to implement a class IntSet that stores a set of integers in a binary search tree.
(a) Write the class declaration with a private nested Node struct, a constructor, a destructor, and public member functions insert(int), contains(int) const, size() const and height() const. Explain why copying must be either disabled or implemented carefully. [8]
(b) Implement insert recursively and contains iteratively. [7]
(c) Implement height and the destructor. [4]
(d) The keys 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80, 30 are inserted into an empty IntSet. Give size(), height(), contains(40) and contains(45). Then give height() after inserting 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 into a new IntSet, and discuss what this means for performance. [6]
markScheme: (a) Private Node {int key; Node* left; Node* right;}, root pointer and count; public interface with const on query functions

(a) Explains that the default copy would copy only the root pointer (shallow copy), so two objects share nodes and both destructors delete them (double delete); so delete copy operations or write a deep copy (rule of three)
(b) insert: base case creates new node and increments count; recurses left or right; ignores duplicates; returns subtree root
(b) contains: loop from root moving left or right until found or nullptr
(c) height: 0 for nullptr, else 1 + max(left, right); destructor uses post-order deletion
(d) size 7 (duplicate 30 ignored), height 3, contains(40) true, contains(45) false
(d) Sorted insertion gives a chain of height 5; operations become O(n) rather than O(log n); mention balanced trees (std::set/std::map use self-balancing trees) or random insertion order
